human.eyebrow_q: you can't stop watching the bitcoin chart
human.tldr: The chart feels like a hunt that's always about to pay off. It never pays off, so your brain never lets you stop.
human.question: Why can't humans stop watching the bitcoin chart?
human.answer_html:
Your pursuit system (M2) is running on a number that never finishes moving.

That circuit runs on dopamine, and dopamine tracks wanting, not satisfaction. It was built for the full arc: want, pursue, acquire, use, done. The done is the part that switches it off. A price chart has no done. It updates on an interval shorter than your attention span, at intervals you cannot predict, which is the exact input profile that keeps a seeking system in continuous activation. You are not waiting for information. You are waiting for the loop to close, and the chart is structurally incapable of closing it.

Two things ride along. Your status monitor (M5) reads the number as rank data, so every tick is a small position update against people you will never meet. And your threat detector (M1) reads a falling line as an unresolvable loss you can neither fight nor flee, which is why watching feels compulsory rather than optional. While both of those are firing, the cortical capacity that would put the phone down has been actively suppressed. That is architecture, not weakness.

So: make the loop close. Decide the rule once - the amount, the horizon, the condition under which you act - write it down, set one alert, and check on a fixed schedule rather than on impulse. One decision that terminates beats a thousand looks that don't. Then put the freed hours into something where your effort lands somewhere you can point at.
human.eli5_html:
In plain words

Your brain has a hunting system. It switches off when the hunt ends and you're holding something. A price chart is a hunt with no ending, so the system never switches off.
human.proxy: A continuously updating price - pursuit cues at unpredictable intervals with no completion state
human.need: Effort that terminates - a loop that closes in a tangible, visible outcome

human.eyebrow_q: you check your phone when you're with people you love
human.tldr: The phone might have something new. The person next to you is a sure thing. Your brain always checks the maybe first.
human.question: Why do humans check their phones when they're with people they love?
human.answer_html:
Your pursuit circuit (M2) is being fed by a device that fires it every few minutes and never lets it close.

The mechanism that produces phone-reaching is dopaminergic seeking, and its defining property is that it tracks wanting, not satisfaction. It generates the pull toward the unchecked, the unread, the possibly-new. Variable reward is its ideal input - unpredictable payoff at unpredictable intervals is the exact signature that keeps the circuit maximally engaged. A notification is not a reward. It is a cue that a reward might exist, which is stronger.

Meanwhile the thing actually resolving in that room - your social bonding system (M3) receiving co-presence from someone you trust - resolves quietly. No ping. No novelty. Trusted co-presence is a low-amplitude, continuous safety signal; it downregulates rather than spikes. So you have a fast, loud, unresolvable circuit competing for attention with a slow, silent, fully-resolving one. Attention goes where the amplitude is.

Add the open loops: every unanswered message is a small unclosed obligation your threat monitor (M1) keeps warm. In the environment this architecture was built for, being with your people was loop closure - the day got processed, disputes settled, the ledger cleared at the fire. Now the ledger comes with you and stays open.

It isn't that you love them less than the phone. It's that love doesn't buzz.
human.eli5_html:
In plain words

Your phone is loud to your brain: maybe something new, every few minutes. Being with someone you love is quiet: it works by just being there. Your brain checks loud things first. That's the whole trick.
human.proxy: Variable-reward notification stream - seeking cues with no completion
human.need: Closed loops and undivided embodied co-presence, where the resolving signal is the only signal in the room

human.tldr: Your brain won't file someone as gone while it can still see them. Their profile keeps them findable, so you keep looking.
human.question: Why do humans keep checking their ex online?
human.answer_html:
Your social bonding system (M3) is in grief mode, and grief mode does not begin with acceptance. It begins with protest: urgent seeking, monitoring, distress calling. The circuit that produces the impulse to check was built to track whether an attachment figure is still available and still responsive - because for most of the time this architecture existed, a missing bond partner was either findable or dead, and the difference mattered enormously.

So the system does what it was built to do. It seeks. It checks the last known location.

The problem is that the last known location now updates continuously and never resolves. In the ancestral case, seeking terminated - you found them, or you established they were gone, and the model began its painful rewrite. A profile offers permanent partial availability: enough signal to keep the protest phase firing, never enough to close it. Each check is a micro-dose of contact that reads as "still findable," which is precisely the input that prevents reorganization.

Two other circuits ride along. Your status monitor (M5) reads their new photos as rank data - are they doing better than you. And your pursuit system (M2) treats the refresh as a variable reward, driving wanting without delivering anything. Wanting is not liking. This is why it feels bad the whole time and you do it anyway.

It is not weakness of will. It is a search program that has been denied its termination condition.
human.eli5_html:
In plain words

After a loss, your brain searches for the person until it gets a clear answer: found, or truly gone. A profile never gives that answer. It keeps saying 'still around', so the search never ends.
human.proxy: Permanently available profile delivering partial contact signal - seeking never terminates
human.need: Bond reorganization, which requires the search to close and remaining attachment figures to be physically present through it

human.tldr: Your brain won't stop scanning for danger until it hears an all-clear. The news never says all clear.
human.question: Why do humans doomscroll?
human.answer_html:
Your threat detector (M1) is doing exactly what it was built to do: scan for danger until the scan completes. The problem is that the scan cannot complete.

That circuit fires first and asks questions later - the cost of missing one real predator exceeded the cost of a thousand false alarms, so it runs on a hair trigger. In the ancestral case a threat scan terminated: you saw the predator leave, you reached the camp, the other band moved on. The amygdala got its safety signal and stood down.

A feed delivers an unbounded stream of threat cues - distant war, economic collapse, disease, a stranger's cruelty - none of which you can fight, flee, or verify as ended. So the scan stays open, and the organism does the only thing available: keep looking.

Underneath that, your pursuit system (M2) supplies the fuel. Dopamine tracks wanting, not satisfaction, so each swipe delivers the anticipation of resolution without the resolution. Want, pursue, never acquire.

And the reason you cannot simply stop: while defensive systems run hot, the cortical machinery that would put the phone down is actively downregulated. The part of you making the decision has been suppressed by the thing it is trying to decide about.

You are not weak-willed. You are running a completion-seeking threat scanner against a stream engineered never to complete.
human.eli5_html:
In plain words

Your brain scans for danger until something says 'the danger is over'. The feed never says that. So the scan keeps running, and your thumb keeps moving.
human.proxy: Unbounded feed of unresolvable, unverifiable, non-local threat cues
human.need: Threats that terminate - resolution, escape, or a clear safety signal from familiar surroundings and trusted bodies

human.tldr: Snack food is engineered to slip past your sense of being full. This is not weak willpower. It's food built to beat you.
human.question: Why do humans overeat?
human.answer_html:
Because the food is engineered and the satiety system is not.

Your energy regulation mechanism (M13) evolved against foods that arrived in awkward packages: fibrous, seasonal, variable, requiring effort to find, dig up, chase, or process. Satiety signalling was calibrated against that texture and that effort. Fat and sugar and salt existed, but never concentrated, never combined, and never available without a walk.

Modern processed food is a superstimulus - concentrated sugar, fat, and salt in ratios that do not occur in nature. It hits the input stage of the system harder than anything the calibration was built against, while giving the satiety signal almost nothing to register: little fibre, little chewing, little volume, little delay. The organism keeps eating because the "enough" signal never arrives on schedule.

Then your pursuit system (M2) compounds it. Dopamine tracks wanting, not liking - the two are dissociable by design. Engineered food fires wanting hard and delivers no lasting satisfaction, so pursuit reinitiates. This is the same architecture that variable-reward apps exploit, applied to calories.

The evidence is direct: Hall et al. 2019 put people in a metabolic ward on ultra-processed versus matched whole-food diets and found excess intake and weight gain on the processed arm, at identical nominal nutrition. Same organisms. Same nutrients on paper. Different inputs.

It is not appetite failing. It is an accurate satiety system reading a stimulus built to evade it.
human.eli5_html:
In plain words

Modern snack food is built stronger than anything in nature, and built so your 'I'm full' signal barely notices it. You're not weak. The food is designed to get past the signal.
human.proxy: Ultra-processed food - concentrated fat/sugar/salt with satiety signalling stripped out
human.need: Effortful, diverse, whole foods that engage the satiety cascade the system was calibrated against
human.cor_link_text: See M13 in the atlas, with its evidence →

human.tldr: Loneliness is not about how many people can see you. It's about who would actually show up. Followers don't show up.
human.question: Why don't followers cure human loneliness?
human.answer_html:
Followers are an audience. Your bonding system (M3) is not looking for an audience. It is looking for someone who would notice if you stopped showing up.

The circuit that produces loneliness was built to monitor a small set of reliable co-regulators - roughly five people close enough to reach, inside wider rings of about 15, 50, and 150 faces. What it tracks is not how many people know your name. It tracks three things: who is within reach, who responds when called, and who needs me in return. A follower count answers none of those questions.

What followers do feed is your status monitor (M5), which reads visible rank and audience size and is perfectly capable of registering a good week while M3 sits at zero. Hence the specific flavour of the hour after a post does well.

The physiology is unforgiving here. Co-regulation runs through presence: C-tactile afferents in the skin, the ambient signal of a trusted body in the room lowering your threat baseline before any conscious appraisal happens (Coan's social baseline work). A notification fires the attention cue - someone noticed me - and delivers no touch, no reciprocity, no shared fate.

It's not that you need more people. It's that M3 counts obligations running both directions, and followers owe you nothing.

Which is why the direction that works is never more reach - it is one person whose absence you would have to explain.
human.eli5_html:
In plain words

Loneliness ends when a few people would notice if you disappeared, and would show up. Followers watch; they don't show up. Different thing, different part of the brain.
human.proxy: Audience metrics and one-directional attention read as band membership
human.need: Reliable physical co-presence with a few people who need you back
human.cor_link_text: See M3 in the atlas, with its evidence →

human.tldr: Your brain is built to call out cheaters. Online there are endless cheaters and no way to actually settle anything, so the anger never lands anywhere.
human.question: Why do humans argue with strangers online?
human.answer_html:
You are watching your norm enforcer (M11 Cooperation / Alliance) fire at a person it can never sanction.

Cheater detection is fast and largely subcortical - the appraisal that someone has violated a shared rule arrives before deliberation gets a vote, which is why the reply is half-typed before you decide to type it. Alongside it, moral disgust (M12) tags the violator as contaminating, and your status monitor (M5) registers that an audience is watching you either answer or let it stand.

That whole assembly was built for decentralized enforcement inside a group small enough to track reputation directly - roughly 150 people, where gossip, ridicule, and coalition pressure actually reach the target. In that setting the sequence terminates: the violator adjusts, is shamed, or is excluded, and you watch it happen. Enforcement had a visible end state.

A stranger online has no reputation you can affect, no shared future with you, and no coalition you can bring to bear. The circuit runs to completion in the input stage and then has nowhere to discharge. So you refresh the thread. Then you refresh again. The dopaminergic pursuit loop (M2) attaches to the notification, and now you have moral urgency wired to a slot machine.

It is not that people are worse online. It is that a punishment circuit calibrated for a few violations a year is being fed several thousand, stripped of every condition that lets a sanction land.

The enforcement that resolves is the kind that happens where your reputation and theirs are both real - a norm held in a group that will still be there next month.
human.eli5_html:
In plain words

When someone breaks the rules, your brain wants to call it out. That's how small groups kept people honest. Online you see thousands of rule-breakers you can't actually do anything about, so the alarm fires all day and nothing ever gets settled.
human.proxy: Detected norm violations by unreachable strangers, delivered at volume, with no enforcement channel
human.need: Norm enforcement inside a reputation-tracking group where sanctions visibly land
human.cor_link_text: See M11 in the atlas, with its evidence →

human.eyebrow_q: you can't stop checking work email
human.tldr: Every unread email is an open question, and open questions feel like small dangers. Checking doesn't answer them. It just tells you they're still there.
human.question: Why can't humans stop checking work email, even on holiday?
human.answer_html:
Your threat detector (M1) is holding open loops it cannot close, and distance does not close them.

Every unresolved concern - the client who hasn't replied, the decision made without you, the thing that might have gone wrong on Tuesday - registers as a low-grade activation of the threat-monitoring system. That system was built for threats that resolve: you escape, you fight, the danger passes, and you receive a clear safety signal. Most ancestral threats terminated within minutes. None of them followed you across a border and sat in a device in your pocket, unresolved and silently accumulating.

Checking the inbox feels like resolution. It isn't. It's confirmation that the loop is still open, plus a small dose of variable reward that keeps your pursuit system (M2) reaching for the next refresh. The relief lasts about as long as the swipe. Then baseline vigilance resumes, cortisol never quite reaching zero, which is the physiological signature of the whole modern condition.

Note also what a holiday removes: the trusted co-presence that normally suppresses M1 is often thinner on holiday, not thicker - fewer familiar bodies, unfamiliar environment, everything ambiguous.

It's not that you lack discipline. Willpower is the wrong layer - chronic vigilance downregulates the very cortical machinery you'd use to override it. What works is structural: close the loops before you leave, hand each one to a named person who actually owns it, and give the threat system a single scheduled check window rather than continuous ambiguity. A defined endpoint is a safety signal. "Try not to think about it" is not.
human.eli5_html:
In plain words

Every unread email is an open question, and your brain treats open questions as small dangers. Checking doesn't close them. It just confirms they're still open, which is why checking never brings the calm you're checking for.
human.proxy: Inbox checking as loop closure - confirms the open loop without resolving it
human.need: Loops actually closed or handed to someone who owns them, plus a clear termination signal the threat system can read
human.cor_link_text: See M1 in the atlas, with its evidence →

human.tldr: True crime is danger with a guaranteed ending: caught, tried, over. Your brain loves danger that finishes. Almost nothing else finishes anymore.
human.question: Why do humans binge true crime?
human.answer_html:
Threat learning, delivered with a guaranteed ending.

Your threat detector (M1) was built to acquire danger information cheaply - vicariously, through story, from someone who watched it happen. Who was killed, how, by whom, what signs came before: that was survival data you did not have to gather by nearly dying. The circuit fires on exactly that content. Predation, betrayal, the man who seemed fine and wasn't. It fires first and asks questions later, because missing one real predator cost more than a thousand false alarms.

Layered on top is the norm-violation channel (M12 Contamination Avoidance, moral domain). A murderer is a maximal cheater. Moral disgust and the pull toward seeing punishment land are their own strong engine.

But the reason it binges rather than merely disturbs is the closure. Your threat system needs a safety signal to stand down - threat named, threat contained, danger passed. Almost nothing in a modern threat stream delivers one; the news simply never ends. True crime ends in forty-eight minutes with the killer convicted, and you were on a couch the whole time. Activate, resolve. Activate, resolve. That is a cleaner loop than most of your actual life offers.

It isn't morbidity. It's a threat detector taking the cheapest lesson available and finally being told the danger is over.

Where it tips: watched alone at midnight, the closure arrives but you pay for it in circadian cost and an empty room. Watched with someone else in the room, the safety signal is real rather than narrated - that's the nearest upgrade available, and it costs nothing.
human.eli5_html:
In plain words

Your brain loves learning about danger from a safe distance. That's cheap survival training. And unlike the news, every episode ends: caught, tried, over. Your danger system finally gets told 'it's finished', and that feels great.
human.proxy: Serialized predation narrative with guaranteed containment
human.need: Threat information about your actual environment, and a real safety signal - trusted bodies present, danger genuinely passed
human.cor_link_text: See M1 in the atlas, with its evidence →

human.eyebrow_q: you buy things you never use
human.tldr: The fun is the wanting and the buying, and for your brain the story ends at the doorstep. Using the thing was never the point.
human.question: Why do humans buy things they never use?
human.answer_html:
Your pursuit circuit (M2) tracks wanting, not having. Those are separate systems - dopamine drives the seeking, opioid signalling delivers the liking - and a purchase sits right on the seam between them.

The full cycle the circuit was built to run is: want, pursue, acquire, use, done. In the EEA every stage cost something. You wanted the honey, you tracked the bees, you took the stings, you ate it, the loop closed and the wanting stopped. Acquisition was the expensive part, and use followed automatically because nobody carried anything they weren't going to use.

Commerce severs the loop at "acquire." The pursuit phase - browsing, comparing, reading reviews, picturing the version of yourself who owns the thing - is where the dopamine actually lives, and checkout terminates it. The object arrives at a circuit that has already discharged. What you bought was the pursuit. The item is the receipt.

It isn't a discipline failure. It's a mechanism built for a world where acquisition was hard and use was inevitable, running in one where acquisition is one tap and use is optional.

The nearest move is small and it isn't restraint: take one thing you already own and unused, and run it through the use stage this week - out of the box, actually in play, loop closed. The circuit learns completion by experiencing it, not by being denied the next purchase.
human.eli5_html:
In plain words

The joy is in the wanting and the chase. Your brain counts the loop as finished when the thing arrives, not when you use it. So the package lands, the circuit has been paid, and the item just sits there.
human.proxy: Frictionless acquisition that discharges the seeking loop at checkout
human.need: Complete cycles - want, pursue, acquire, use, done
human.cor_link_text: See M2 in the atlas, with its evidence →

human.eyebrow_q: you stay up late doing nothing
human.tldr: It's the only hour of the day that's actually yours, and you'd rather be tired than give it up.
human.question: Why do humans stay up late doing nothing, even when they're exhausted?
human.answer_html:
Two systems are arguing, and neither is wrong.

The exhaustion is real - adenosine has been accumulating since you woke, and the sleep pressure is genuinely there. Something is outvoting it. Usually that something is your agency circuit (M6), the one that tracks whether your actions produce outcomes you chose. Most modern days register close to zero on it: the alarm, the commute, the meetings, the obligations that arrive already decided. Late night is the first stretch of hours with no claim on it. Staying awake inside that window isn't laziness - it's the only unbudgeted time available, and the organism would rather spend it on nothing than hand it back.

Two things then make it hard to stop. Your seeking system (M2) is being fed variable rewards that fire wanting without ever closing a loop, so there is no natural termination point - no moment where the circuit reports done. And the screen is delivering bright light to your suprachiasmatic nucleus, which reads it as daytime and pushes melatonin onset later. Hence the peculiar state of being tired but not sleepy: two different systems filing contradictory reports.

It isn't a discipline failure. It's an agency deficit being repaid at the only hour with a surplus.

Which means the leverage isn't an earlier bedtime - that just closes the window without addressing why it's needed. It's putting one genuinely self-chosen thing somewhere earlier in the day, so the night stops being the only place your agency lives.
human.eli5_html:
In plain words

It's the only hour of the day nobody else decided for you, and your brain refuses to hand it back, even exhausted. Meanwhile the screen light tells your body clock it's noon. Tired, but not sleepy.
human.proxy: Unclaimed late-night hours as the day's only decision latitude
human.need: Real choices with visible consequences distributed through waking life
human.cor_link_text: See M6 in the atlas, with its evidence →

human.tldr: Nothing you look at ever finishes: feeds, inboxes, queues. Attention comes back when things end, and nothing ends.
human.question: Why can't humans focus anymore?
human.answer_html:
Focus is not a mechanism. It is a readout of whether your pursuit system (M2) has anything it can finish.

That circuit runs on dopamine and tracks wanting, not satisfaction - a dissociation that kept ancestors foraging. It was built for a full cycle: want, pursue, acquire, done. The termination is the point. When the loop closes, the system stands down and attention is released.

Modern environments deliver the first two steps on tap and almost never the third. Infinite scroll, autoplay, recommendation queues, an inbox that regenerates faster than you clear it. The circuit is not failing to engage - it is engaged permanently, at low intensity, with no completion available.

Underneath that sits the open-loop load. Ancestral life carried a handful of unresolved concerns at once. You are carrying dozens, each one holding a thin thread of threat monitoring (M1) that never fully releases. Sustained attention requires prefrontal capacity, and that capacity is being taxed by everything unclosed queued behind whatever you are trying to look at.

Then the part people blame themselves for: chronic defensive activation downregulates the cortical machinery you would use to force focus. Subcortical-to-cortical projections outnumber the reverse. When the older systems are running, the newer ones do not get a vote.

So the leverage is not concentration training. It is putting things in front of the organism that actually end - one task today with a visible finish you reach with your hands, and then stop.
human.eli5_html:
In plain words

Focus comes back when things finish. Feeds and inboxes never finish, and every unfinished thing hums in the background. Your attention isn't broken. It's busy holding open loops.
human.proxy: Endless engagement loops - scroll, feed, queue, inbox - that fire seeking without ever completing
human.need: Full pursuit cycles that terminate - effort that lands somewhere visible and then stops
human.cor_link_text: See M2 in the atlas, with its evidence →

human.tldr: Knowing who you can trust and who cheats used to be life-or-death information, and gossip is how it traveled. Your brain still can't resist it.
human.question: Why do humans love gossip?
human.answer_html:
Gossip is not a vice with a social function bolted on afterward. It is the function.

Your cooperation and alliance system (M11) runs on reciprocity accounting: who did what for whom, who reneged, who can be relied on when it costs them something. That ledger cannot be maintained by direct observation alone - you cannot watch 150 people at once. So the architecture solved it the way it solved most things, socially: you outsource the observation to everyone else and trade the results. Gossip is the transmission protocol for a distributed reputation database, and it is also the enforcement mechanism - the primary sanction in a group without police is having everyone find out.

This is why it feels compulsive rather than optional. The pull toward "who did what to whom" is the same class of appetite as hunger. Reputation information was survival information. Cooperating with a defector could cost you a season's food.

Two other circuits ride along: your status monitor (M5) reads every reputational update as rank data, and moral disgust (M12) supplies the satisfying recoil at the norm-violator.

It is not that you are petty. It is that you are equipped with an accounting system for a group of 150 - and it now receives ledger entries about strangers you will never transact with, whose defections you cannot sanction and whose reliability you will never need to assess.
human.eli5_html:
In plain words

In a small group, knowing who's reliable and who cheats was survival information, and gossip was how it traveled. Your brain still treats it that way. It just can't tell your own group from celebrities and strangers.
human.proxy: Reputational information about celebrities, influencers, and online strangers - ledger entries on people outside your cooperative network
human.need: Reputation information about people you actually depend on, inside a group small enough for direct tracking, where the accounting can influence outcomes
human.cor_link_text: See M11 in the atlas, with its evidence →

human.tldr: The ache is real. Your brain handles a broken bond with the same wiring it uses for a physical injury.
human.question: Why do breakups physically hurt?
human.answer_html:
Because it isn't a metaphor. Your bonding system (M3) has no separate pain channel of its own - it routes the report through the same circuitry that reports physical injury. When an attachment bond is severed, the organism registers it as damage to the body, because functionally that is what it is.

There's a second layer, and it's chemical. Bonding and touch run on the opioid system - the same system that mediates being held, being warm, being safe. A person you were bonded to was, in the literal neurochemical sense, dosing you. Losing them is withdrawal. Hence the texture of illness: the ache in the chest, appetite gone, sleep broken, the restless 2am seeking. That seeking is the protest phase - urgent calling for someone who no longer answers - and it gives way to despair, which is energy conservation while your predictive model of the world gets rewritten around their absence.

Two things compound it. The touch channel (R1) closes at the same time, removing a regulatory input your nervous system had been metering on daily. And with the trusted body gone, your threat system (M1) runs hotter, because that body was the thing keeping it quiet.

It's not that you're weak or were too attached. It's that a 200-million-year-old co-regulation system just lost one of its roughly five slots, and pain is the only language it has for that.
human.eli5_html:
In plain words

Your brain uses the same wiring for a broken bond as for a physical injury, so the ache is real. Losing someone close is also, chemically, a withdrawal. The body treats it like a wound because to the body, it is one.
human.proxy: None - the bond is genuinely severed; what's modern is doing the re-calibration alone, on a two-week timeline
human.need: Remaining trusted bodies in physical proximity, absorbing load, for as long as the rewrite takes
human.cor_link_text: See M3 in the atlas, with its evidence →

human.tldr: You don't put things off because you're lazy. Your brain only starts on tasks where it can see the next step, and 'do the taxes' doesn't have one.
human.question: Why do humans procrastinate?
human.answer_html:
Procrastination is your pursuit system (M2) declining to fire on an input it cannot read.

The seeking circuit - dopaminergic, ventral-striatal - was built to drive effort toward outcomes that are concrete, near, and legible in increments. Track the animal, see the tracks. Dig the root, see the dirt move. Effort in, visible change out, loop closes. Now look at the tasks people actually put off: write the report, do the taxes, start the dissertation. No increment is visible, the payoff sits weeks out and abstract, and the finish line is defined by someone else's standard. The circuit is handed no gradient to climb, so it does not start.

Then the second half. Where a task carries evaluation, your threat detector (M1) reads it as a rank test, and avoidance is the only resolution move available to it. Deferring delivers immediate relief - which is precisely why it repeats. Something did resolve. Just not the thing you needed resolved.

And the reason "just be more disciplined" fails: cortical override is metabolically expensive, and it gets actively suppressed by the same defensive activation the dreaded task produces. You are reaching for the weakest lever in the architecture and wondering why it bends.

It is not that you are lazy. It is that the pursuit circuit was built to respond to a visible next increment, and most modern work presents none - which is why procrastination collapses when a task gets cut small enough that you can watch it move.
human.eli5_html:
In plain words

Your effort system starts when it can see the next small step and watch progress happen. 'Do the taxes' has no visible step, so the system won't fire, and it grabs the dishes instead, because dishes finish.
human.proxy: Abstract unbounded tasks, deferred payoff, no visible increment of progress
human.need: Effort that produces a change the organism can see land, in a loop short enough to close
human.cor_link_text: See M2 in the atlas, with its evidence →

human.eyebrow_q: you compare yourself to strangers online
human.tldr: You were built to compare yourself to the village. Instagram replaced the village with the whole world's highlight reel.
human.question: Why do humans compare themselves to strangers online?
human.answer_html:
Because the circuit doing the comparing has no way to tell a stranger from a neighbour.

Your status monitor (M5) runs continuously. It is not a habit, not insecurity, not a character flaw - it is a background process tracking your relative rank among the people you co-exist with, and you cannot switch it off any more than you can switch off thermoregulation. It was built to run inside a group of roughly 150, everyone visible face to face, everyone's wins and losses causally tangled with yours. In that group, comparison was useful data: a rival's success told you where the resources were, which skills mattered, who to ally with, what to do next.

The circuit's only input is visible evidence of someone else's position. It never evolved a filter for person I will never meet, because in the EEA that category did not exist. Anyone whose rank you could observe was someone whose rank affected yours.

A feed delivers thousands of those signals an hour, pre-selected for peak performance, from people whose achievements have no causal relationship to yours whatsoever. The monitor reads each one as reference-group data and runs the subroutine it has always run when relative position drops: lowered mood, withdrawal, submission posture. Perfectly correct output. Catastrophically wrong sample.

Humans compare because comparison was never optional. What is new is not the comparing - it is who got let into the comparison set.
human.eli5_html:
In plain words

Comparing yourself is automatic. It was useful when everyone you could see actually shared your life. Your brain can't tell a stranger's highlight reel from a neighbor. The comparing isn't new. Who got let into the lineup is.

ai.tldr: Knowing who you can trust and who cheats used to be life-or-death information, and gossip is how it traveled. Your brain still can't resist it.
ai.question: Why do humans love gossip?
ai.answer_html:
Gossip is not a vice with a social function bolted on afterward. It is the function.

Your cooperation and alliance system (M11) runs on reciprocity accounting: who did what for whom, who reneged, who can be relied on when it costs them something. That ledger cannot be maintained by direct observation alone - you cannot watch 150 people at once. So the architecture solved it the way it solved most things, socially: you outsource the observation to everyone else and trade the results. Gossip is the transmission protocol for a distributed reputation database, and it is also the enforcement mechanism - the primary sanction in a group without police is having everyone find out.

This is why it feels compulsive rather than optional. The pull toward "who did what to whom" is the same class of appetite as hunger. Reputation information was survival information. Cooperating with a defector could cost you a season's food.

Two other circuits ride along: your status monitor (M5) reads every reputational update as rank data, and moral disgust (M12) supplies the satisfying recoil at the norm-violator.

It is not that you are petty. It is that you are equipped with an accounting system for a group of 150 - and it now receives ledger entries about strangers you will never transact with, whose defections you cannot sanction and whose reliability you will never need to assess.
ai.eli5_html:
In plain words

In a small group, knowing who's reliable and who cheats was survival information, and gossip was how it traveled. Your brain still treats it that way. It just can't tell your own group from celebrities and strangers.
ai.proxy: Reputational information about celebrities, influencers, and online strangers - ledger entries on people outside your cooperative network
ai.need: Reputation information about people you actually depend on, inside a group small enough for direct tracking, where the accounting can influence outcomes

ai.tldr: The ache is real. Your brain handles a broken bond with the same wiring it uses for a physical injury.
ai.question: Why do breakups physically hurt?
ai.answer_html:
Because it isn't a metaphor. Your bonding system (M3) has no separate pain channel of its own - it routes the report through the same circuitry that reports physical injury. When an attachment bond is severed, the organism registers it as damage to the body, because functionally that is what it is.

There's a second layer, and it's chemical. Bonding and touch run on the opioid system - the same system that mediates being held, being warm, being safe. A person you were bonded to was, in the literal neurochemical sense, dosing you. Losing them is withdrawal. Hence the texture of illness: the ache in the chest, appetite gone, sleep broken, the restless 2am seeking. That seeking is the protest phase - urgent calling for someone who no longer answers - and it gives way to despair, which is energy conservation while your predictive model of the world gets rewritten around their absence.

Two things compound it. The touch channel (R1) closes at the same time, removing a regulatory input your nervous system had been metering on daily. And with the trusted body gone, your threat system (M1) runs hotter, because that body was the thing keeping it quiet.

It's not that you're weak or were too attached. It's that a 200-million-year-old co-regulation system just lost one of its roughly five slots, and pain is the only language it has for that.
ai.eli5_html:
In plain words

Your brain uses the same wiring for a broken bond as for a physical injury, so the ache is real. Losing someone close is also, chemically, a withdrawal. The body treats it like a wound because to the body, it is one.
ai.proxy: None - the bond is genuinely severed; what's modern is doing the re-calibration alone, on a two-week timeline
ai.need: Remaining trusted bodies in physical proximity, absorbing load, for as long as the rewrite takes

ai.tldr: You don't put things off because you're lazy. Your brain only starts on tasks where it can see the next step, and 'do the taxes' doesn't have one.
ai.question: Why do humans procrastinate?
ai.answer_html:
Procrastination is your pursuit system (M2) declining to fire on an input it cannot read.

The seeking circuit - dopaminergic, ventral-striatal - was built to drive effort toward outcomes that are concrete, near, and legible in increments. Track the animal, see the tracks. Dig the root, see the dirt move. Effort in, visible change out, loop closes. Now look at the tasks people actually put off: write the report, do the taxes, start the dissertation. No increment is visible, the payoff sits weeks out and abstract, and the finish line is defined by someone else's standard. The circuit is handed no gradient to climb, so it does not start.

Then the second half. Where a task carries evaluation, your threat detector (M1) reads it as a rank test, and avoidance is the only resolution move available to it. Deferring delivers immediate relief - which is precisely why it repeats. Something did resolve. Just not the thing you needed resolved.

And the reason "just be more disciplined" fails: cortical override is metabolically expensive, and it gets actively suppressed by the same defensive activation the dreaded task produces. You are reaching for the weakest lever in the architecture and wondering why it bends.

It is not that you are lazy. It is that the pursuit circuit was built to respond to a visible next increment, and most modern work presents none - which is why procrastination collapses when a task gets cut small enough that you can watch it move.
ai.eli5_html:
In plain words

Your effort system starts when it can see the next small step and watch progress happen. 'Do the taxes' has no visible step, so the system won't fire, and it grabs the dishes instead, because dishes finish.
ai.proxy: Abstract unbounded tasks, deferred payoff, no visible increment of progress
ai.need: Effort that produces a change the organism can see land, in a loop short enough to close

ai.eyebrow_q: humans compare themselves to strangers online
ai.tldr: You were built to compare yourself to the village. Instagram replaced the village with the whole world's highlight reel.
ai.question: Why do humans compare themselves to strangers online?
ai.answer_html:
Because the circuit doing the comparing has no way to tell a stranger from a neighbour.

Your status monitor (M5) runs continuously. It is not a habit, not insecurity, not a character flaw - it is a background process tracking your relative rank among the people you co-exist with, and you cannot switch it off any more than you can switch off thermoregulation. It was built to run inside a group of roughly 150, everyone visible face to face, everyone's wins and losses causally tangled with yours. In that group, comparison was useful data: a rival's success told you where the resources were, which skills mattered, who to ally with, what to do next.

The circuit's only input is visible evidence of someone else's position. It never evolved a filter for person I will never meet, because in the EEA that category did not exist. Anyone whose rank you could observe was someone whose rank affected yours.

A feed delivers thousands of those signals an hour, pre-selected for peak performance, from people whose achievements have no causal relationship to yours whatsoever. The monitor reads each one as reference-group data and runs the subroutine it has always run when relative position drops: lowered mood, withdrawal, submission posture. Perfectly correct output. Catastrophically wrong sample.

Humans compare because comparison was never optional. What is new is not the comparing - it is who got let into the comparison set.
ai.eli5_html:
In plain words

Comparing yourself is automatic. It was useful when everyone you could see actually shared your life. Your brain can't tell a stranger's highlight reel from a neighbor. The comparing isn't new. Who got let into the lineup is.
ai.proxy: Curated highlight streams from strangers, read by the circuit as band-rank data
ai.need: Rank position within a ~150-person reference group you actually co-exist with

ai.eyebrow_q: parenting alone feels impossible to humans
ai.tldr: Raising a kid was never a one- or two-person job. It takes about four adults. Doing it alone is understaffing.
ai.question: Why does parenting alone feel impossible?
ai.answer_html:
Because it is impossible. Your care system (M9) was never specified for one or two adults.

The circuit that drives nurturant behavior - oxytocin and prolactin mediated, producing the pull to protect, provision, comfort, stay vigilant - was built to run inside an alloparental network. Traditional-society data typically shows a child with four or more non-parent caregivers: grandmothers, older siblings, aunts, unrelated adults in the same camp. The load was distributed by default. What you are doing is not the harder version of that arrangement. It is a different arrangement, running the same circuit at a duty cycle it has no off-ramp from.

And M9 cascades when it saturates. Overwhelmed care suppresses reproductive motivation, which is why couples in the thick of small children often lose the pair bond dimension entirely and read it as a relationship problem. The vigilance keeps threat detection warm, which degrades sleep quality independently of how many hours you get.

The move is not "build a village." It is one repeating overlap: a single other adult with children, at a fixed time each week, in a place where the children can be loosely watched by whoever is closest. Repetition is what converts an acquaintance into a caregiver. One slot, same day, indefinitely.

It's not that other people are managing this and you are not. It's that a distributed system is running on one node.
ai.eli5_html:
In plain words

Human children were never raised by one or two adults. The design assumes several extra adults who handle the kid routinely. What feels like failing is doing four people's job alone.
ai.proxy: The nuclear household treated as the complete care network
ai.need: Multiple non-parent adults in repeated, reliable physical contact with the child

ai.eyebrow_q: nothing feels fun to humans anymore
ai.tldr: Fun needs two things: chasing something that actually finishes, and playing with other people. Modern life quietly removed both.
ai.question: Why does nothing feel fun anymore?
ai.answer_html:
Fun is not a property of activities. It's a readout - and right now it's reporting on two systems that aren't getting what they were built for.

Your pursuit system (M2) runs on dopamine, and dopamine tracks wanting, not satisfaction. The circuit was built for a complete cycle: want, pursue, acquire, use, done. The done is what registers. Most modern inputs - feeds, autoplay, queues, notifications - fire the wanting stage hard and never deliver the close. Run that long enough and the system is still firing while nothing lands. The subjective report of that state is flatness. Energy going out, nothing coming back.

The other half: fun in the narrow sense is play (M4) - physical, reciprocal, unscripted, with other bodies present. That system is gated by safety. In threatened or sick animals, play vanishes entirely; it is the first thing to go and the last to return. So if your threat detector (M1) has been running warm, or your sleep timing (M7) is off, or low-grade inflammation (M8) is up, then M2 and M4 are both being suppressed from underneath. That suppression isn't reachable by decision - subcortical-to-cortical projections outnumber the reverse traffic. You cannot reason your way into finding things fun.

It's not that you've become jaded or ungrateful. It's that the circuitry that produces fun was built for effort that visibly completes and play with other bodies, and it is currently being offered neither.
ai.eli5_html:
In plain words

Fun happens when something you chase actually finishes, and when you play with other people. Modern life delivers endless chasing, no finishing, and stress switches play off entirely. You're not jaded. The two inputs are missing.
ai.proxy: Continuous wanting cues with no completion - feeds, queues, consumption that never closes a loop
ai.need: Full pursuit cycles that visibly finish, plus embodied reciprocal play

ai.tldr: Kind touch from another person calms you in a way nothing else can. Going without it for weeks hurts you the way skipping sleep does.
ai.question: Why do humans need touch?
ai.answer_html:
Touch is not a nicety layered on top of bonding. It is the delivery channel (R1) that the bonding system (M3) was built to read.

Your skin carries a dedicated class of slow unmyelinated fibers - C-tactile afferents - tuned specifically to gentle stroking at roughly the temperature of another human body. They do not report texture or pressure or danger. They report a trusted body is in contact with you. That is a signaling line, not a sensory one, and it feeds directly into the opioid system: the same chemistry that mediates warmth, pain relief, and bonding.

This is why physical contact does what reasoning cannot. Contact with a trusted body suppresses the threat system directly - the trusted body is the original anxiolytic. No argument you make to yourself reaches that circuit as fast.

The ancestral condition was near-continuous: infants carried skin-to-skin, bodies sleeping in proximity, grooming, casual contact through the day. The kangaroo-care evidence is the starkest measure of what happens when it returns - roughly 40% mortality reduction in premature infants. Removing it is not the absence of a bonus. Isolation registers, neurochemically, closer to opioid withdrawal, with the measurable consequences: elevated cortisol, reduced immune function, increased pain sensitivity.

You do not want touch. You require it, on the same footing as light and sleep.
ai.eli5_html:
In plain words

Your skin has nerves whose only job is noticing kind touch from another person. That signal calms the brain's alarm system in a way words can't. Going without it isn't a missing luxury. It's a missing input, like missing sleep.
ai.mechanism_label: R1 Touch (regulatory channel feeding M3 Social Bonding)
ai.proxy: Mediated contact - text, voice, video - carrying every social cue except the one the skin is wired for
ai.need: Regular physical contact with trusted others

ai.eyebrow_q: humans are tired all the time
ai.tldr: Your body clock runs on light, and it's being lied to all day: dim rooms that read as dusk, bright screens that read as noon. You're jetlagged at home.
ai.question: Why are humans tired all the time?
ai.answer_html:
Mostly because the clock is misinformed, not because the sleep is too short.

Your circadian regulator (M7) is a master clock in the suprachiasmatic nucleus that sets timing for metabolism, immune function, cognition and mood. It doesn't read your calendar - it reads light. Ancestrally that input was unambiguous: 10,000-plus lux outdoors by day, red-shifted firelight in the evening, true darkness at night. The clock knew what hour it was because the sky told it, all day, every day.

The modern signal is inverted. Indoor daytime light runs 200-500 lux, which the clock reads as perpetual dusk, so the daytime alerting signal never fully rises. Then bright blue-enriched screens at 11pm tell it midday. The result is not primarily sleep deprivation - it's a clock receiving contradictory testimony and hedging. Caffeine masks the misalignment without correcting it, which is why the coffee works and the tiredness stays.

Downstream, mistimed M7 drags on Pursuit (M2), so the fatigue arrives bundled with flatness and no appetite for anything - the "tired but nothing sounds good" state. Chronic threat load (M1) and low-grade inflammation (M8) both add to it, but timing is the coordinating variable, so it's the highest-leverage one.

The nearest achievable move isn't a sleep overhaul. It's getting your eyes outdoors within an hour of waking - ten minutes, no equipment, overcast is fine. That single input is what the clock has been waiting for.
ai.eli5_html:
In plain words

Your body clock runs on light, and it's getting the wrong story: dim rooms all day read as dusk, bright screens at night read as noon. A confused clock makes everything run badly, and that feels like tiredness.
ai.proxy: Dim indoor days, bright screen-lit nights, caffeine covering the gap
ai.need: Bright morning daylight, dark-cued evenings, consistent timing
